title: Portfolio & annotation
examples: How do I show my development in my portfolio?
What exactly do 'assessment objectives' mean for my art piece?
Should I just write what I did, or what I learned?

explain.say: Today we are looking at building a strong portfolio.
A portfolio collects many pieces of your work together.
Annotation means writing notes on your work itself.
Assessment objectives tell you what skills to focus on.
Developing your work shows how you improved over time.
In real life, a chef keeps a recipe book.

faq.q: Should I annotate every single piece in my portfolio?
faq.a: No, you should annotate the most important pieces. Focus on showing growth or meeting a key objective.

faq.q: What is the difference between describing and evaluating?
faq.a: Describing tells us what you did, and evaluating tells us how well you think it worked and why.
asks: What is the difference between stating and judging?

faq.q: If I change my mind a lot, is that good for my portfolio?
faq.a: Yes, showing changes shows development. Keep those early, failed attempts too.

faq.q: How do I link my annotations to the assessment objectives?
faq.a: You must use the language of the assessment objectives in your writing. Name the skill you are showing.
asks: How do I use the AOs?
Can I just talk about art without mentioning the objectives?

faq.q: Are there rules for how many words I should write?
faq.a: There are no strict word counts, but your writing must be detailed and thoughtful. Quality always beats quantity.

facts: A portfolio is a collection of work showing progress.
Annotation involves writing explanations directly onto the work.
Assessment objectives guide what skills you need to demonstrate.
Development is shown by comparing early ideas to final outcomes.

quiz.say: Which part of the portfolio shows how your skill improved?
quiz.show: Comparing early sketches to final pieces.
quiz.why: Development specifically tracks the journey from an initial idea to a finished product.

wrong.1: Annotation is the writing, not the comparison of pieces.
wrong.2: Assessment objectives are the goals, not the evidence of change.
wrong.3: The portfolio is the container, not the evidence itself.

quiz.say: If an objective is to 'evaluate', what should your writing do?
quiz.show: Judge your work's success and failure.
quiz.why: Evaluation requires making judgments about the quality and effectiveness of your choices.

wrong.0: Planning is looking forward, evaluation looks at the work done.
wrong.1: Listing goals is stating requirements, not judging the outcome.
wrong.3: Describing only lists materials and actions taken.

quiz.say: When annotating, what is the most important thing to include?

options.show: Which assessment objective does this show?
options.say: Which assessment objective does this show?

quiz.why: Always connect your writing back to the specific skill you are supposed to be demonstrating.

wrong.0: Time taken is irrelevant unless the objective is time management.
wrong.1: Your own critical thought is what needs to be recorded.
wrong.3: Materials are facts, but not evidence of skill.
